gglaplot2 is the Greater London Authority's house style for ggplot2. It is
built on the same design tokens, typeface and chart conventions as the City
Intelligence Unit's web charts, taken from the visualisation team's
[ldn-viz-tools](https://github.com/Greater-London-Authority/ldn-viz-tools)
package unchanged, so a chart made here and a chart on one of their sites read
as one system.

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
```

Coming from gglaplot? Its names all still work; the Migrating from gglaplot
page lists what each is now.

## A chart

Three things make a chart: the theme, a mark, and the labels.

```{r first}
a <- gla_monthly[gla_monthly$series == "Variable A", ]

ggplot(a, aes(month, value)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_number()) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Variable A has fallen steadily since 2017",
    subtitle = "London monthly estimated value (GBP), January 2015 to March 2024",
    source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data",
    note = "Data for demonstration only",
    byline = "GLA City Intelligence",
    x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gla()
```

`theme_gla()` draws the non-data ink from the `chart-*` tokens and sets the
type from the design system's chart roles. With ggplot2 4 it also carries the
data defaults, so `geom_gla_line()` is a 2px `data-primary` line without being
told. `gla_labs()` is `labs()` with the eyebrow, title, subtitle, byline,
source and note the web chart container shows, drawn as it draws them: the
eyebrow above the title and the `Source:` and `Note:` labels in bold.

## Series

Colour a series with `scale_colour_gla()`. Its default reads the level names
the way the web charts do: London against a comparator is primary against
context grey, and anything else takes the categorical palette in order. Label
the lines at their ends rather than in a legend.

```{r series}
ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endpoint() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = series)) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.18))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_number()) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Three series", subtitle = "Monthly value, GBP", x = NULL) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## Dark mode

Every mark reads its colour from the theme, and every function that colours
something reads the mode, so one switch changes the whole chart.
`gla_mode("dark")` sets it for the session; `with_gla_mode()` for one chart.

```{r dark}
with_gla_mode("dark", {
  ggplot(gla_yearly, aes(factor(year), average, fill = series)) +
    geom_gla_col() +
    gla_zero_line() +
    scale_fill_gla() +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = label_gla_number(),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
    gla_labs(title = "On an inverse surface", subtitle = "Yearly average, GBP", x = NULL) +
    theme_gla()
})
```

## Saving

`gla_save()` writes the chart at the web charts' size, 880 by 440 pixels,
doubled for a sharp image, through ragg so the bundled Inter is used.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
gla_save(p, "chart.png")
```

## Labels

`label_gla_number()`, `label_gla_percent()`, `label_gla_pounds()` and
`label_gla_date()` put values in the shapes the web charts use, for a
scale's `labels` argument: a comma every three digits, `£` against the
number, whole percentages from fractions and dates written out.
`label_gla_pounds(short = TRUE)` writes `£1.2bn`.

```{r labels}
label_gla_pounds(short = TRUE)(c(45000, 3.5e6, 1.2e9))
label_gla_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(0.123)
label_gla_date()(as.Date("2024-03-05"))
```
